reason: Heart muscle fits the chamber outline and should provide the squeezing force needed for the pump.
expectation: The chambers will gain muscle that can squeeze them.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so valves should direct the flow.
reaction: The two-way flow makes the need for valves clear.
reason: The valve picture shows them closing against reverse flow, which should help drive blood forward.
expectation: The valves will prevent backward flow during a squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refilling; the heart still needs repeated squeezes.
reaction: The paired panels make the valves' role clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells' spreading electrical wave suggests they can coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The pacemaker cells give the heart a coordinated beat, completing the pump goal. The remaining goal needs blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it was useful.
reason: Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites should equip the flexible red-cell envelopes to carry oxygen.
expectation: The envelopes will become oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria; they still need to be combined with plasma for the blood route.
reaction: The contrast with the mitochondria-containing muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The red cells and plasma formed blood, with sugar dissolved in the plasma. The pump and vessel route still need to be connected.
reaction: The picture makes the different roles of plasma and red cells clear.
reason: Capillary networks should connect the branching arteries and veins into a returning route.
expectation: The vessels will form a connected circulation route.

effect: The capillaries connected the arteries and veins into a circuit with slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The labeled slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit’s pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted into the circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is installed in the circuit; the transport medium slot still needs blood.
reaction: The heart's connection to outgoing and returning vessels makes the circuit easier to picture.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the circuit's transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will be fitted into the vessel circuit.

effect: The blood completed the circuit, showing how the pump and vessels can deliver supplies to tissues and return blood for another trip.
reaction: Seeing the separate parts form a closed route was satisfying; the capillary exchange inset connected it back to cellular needs.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile because the before-and-after pictures showed why squeezing alone does not ensure forward flow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart and blood into named slots was clear but predictable once the circuit existed.

surprise.text: The red blood cells' lack of mitochondria, despite still making ATP from sugar, changed my picture of what a working cell needs.

arbitrary.text: No action felt especially arbitrary; the item descriptions and circuit slots gave each combination a recognizable purpose.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the circulation connects with the other systems. The exchange picture raised that question, although assembling the final slots was straightforward.
